lesson.title: Liaison & Silent Consonants: CaReFuL
lesson.subtitle: Why final consonants go silent except C, R, F, L — and wake up before a vowel in liaison (vous avez, les amis).

hook.title: The Sleeping Consonant at the End of the Word
hook.content: Use the English word CaReFuL! If a French word ends in C, R, F, or L (avec, hiver, neuf, hôtel), you usually pronounce that final consonant. If it ends in S, T, D, X, Z, P, N (vous, est, grand, deux, voulez), that final letter sleeps — until the very next word starts with a vowel and wakes it up in liaison!

footnotes.title: Three Liaison Sounds: S/X → /z/, T/D → /t/, N → /n/
footnotes.content: When a consonant wakes up before a vowel: S and X buzz like /z/ (vous‿avez, deux‿ans), T and D tap like /t/ (c'est‿un ami, grand‿hôtel), and N links as /n/ (un‿ami, mon‿ami)!

pattern.title: CaReFuL Finals Stay Awake; S/X, T/D, N Wake Before Vowels
pattern.content: Listen for the consonant bridge jumping across the space onto the next vowel-initial word.
pattern.linguist_note: Word-final consonants survived before vowel-initial words within the same phonological phrase (liaison).
pattern.trap_note: Never pronounce S or X as /s/ in liaison — it ALWAYS buzzes as voiced /z/ (vous‿avez /vu.za.ve/)!

exercises.prompt: Match each linked phrase with its liaison sound:
exercises.meaning: vous‿avez / les‿amis (S before vowel), deux‿ans / six‿heures (X before vowel), c'est‿important (T before vowel), un‿ami / mon‿hôtel (N before vowel)

exercises.prompt: In 'deux ans' ('two years'), how is the final -x of 'deux' pronounced before 'ans'?
exercises.meaning: X wakes up as /z/ before a vowel in liaison
exercises.explanation: Both S and X turn into voiced /z/ before a vowel.

exercises.prompt: Which word below pronounces its final consonant even when standing alone (the CaReFuL rule)?
exercises.meaning: F is in CaReFuL, so neuf (/nœf/) pronounces its final f
exercises.explanation: C, R, F, L are usually pronounced at the end of a word.

exercises.idea: you have two friends here (polite vous)
cues: two friends here → deux amis ici
idea_parts: number + noun + place → deux amis ici
exercises.explanation: Both Vous‿avez and deux‿amis link with a /z/ buzz.

diagnosis.slip: used Tu as instead of Vous avez
diagnosis.cue: Use Vous avez deux amis ici.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.affirmation: You heard the linked words and wrote C'est un bon hôtel cleanly.

summary.outcome: Apply the CaReFuL rule for final consonants and produce /z/, /t/, and /n/ liaisons before vowels.

use_example.german: Vous avez un bon ami à l'hôtel.
use_example.english: You have a good friend at the hotel.

summary.takeaway: Final consonants sleep unless they are CaReFuL — or unless the next word's vowel wakes them up.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([11] Adjectives & the Silent -s): see how Liaison & Silent Consonants: CaReFuL leads directly into Adjectives & the Silent -s.

twist.prompt: Think it through again without looking back — express "You have two friends here" in French:
twist.explanation: Re-constructing "Vous avez deux amis ici" from the underlying rule cements the pattern of Liaison & Silent Consonants: CaReFuL.

vous.etymology_derivation: Latin vōs 'you all' promoted to politeness — the same T–V ladder as German Sie and English's lost 'ye'.

avez.etymology_derivation: In liaison, the s of vous buzzes as /z/: vous‿avez /vu.za.ve/.

êtes.etymology_derivation: Old French estes → êtes: the circumflex hat marks the vanished s.

nous.etymology_derivation: Latin nōs — English keeps the root in nostrum.

ami.etymology_derivation: In liaison, un ami sounds like /œ̃.na.mi/ and mes amis like /me.za.mi/.

hôtel.shift_rule: Norman doublet: S and H dropped
hôtel.etymology_derivation: Latin hospitalis → hostel AND hôtel — the same word entered English twice: once with its S (hostel, hospital), once without (hôtel).

ans.context_translation: I'm thirty years old (I have thirty years).
ans.etymology_derivation: Latin annus — annual, anniversary. Age is something you have in French: j'ai X ans.

bon.etymology_derivation: Latin bonus 'good' — English borrowed the word back as 'bonus', a good thing added.
